lessons.title: Swap Behavior, Not Code
lessons.hook: Same call, different move - that's the whole trick.

blocks.heading: Pick behavior at runtime
blocks.body: When a class must behave differently depending on context, avoid a growing if/else inside it. Instead, define a small interface with one method - the behavior. Write each option as its own class implementing that interface. The class needing the behavior stores a reference to the interface, never to one concrete option, and calls that single method. To change behavior, hand it a different object; nothing inside the class changes. This is the strategy pattern: pick the algorithm at runtime by swapping objects, not editing code. It keeps a class open to new behavior later without touching what already works.

blocks.caption: Static example, no Run button here. Same call, different sound - swap the object, not the class.

steps.say: One shared method means any style can stand in for another without Host knowing which one it got.
Each style is its own small class, so a new one never edits the others.
Host keeps a reference to the interface, never to one style, so it stays unchanged later.
Choosing Formal happens only here - the one place behavior actually gets picked for this run.
Swapping to Casual needs only a new object, proof Host never changed to allow it.

blocks.caption: Same Host, two voices - nothing about Host changes.

blocks.prompt: Same idea, new channels. Trace which object each call goes through before you predict what prints, in order.
blocks.hint: Look at which object n holds at the moment each alert call actually runs, not which one it started with.
blocks.explain: n is reassigned to a new Notifier before the second alert, so the second line comes from Email, not Sms.

blocks.prompt: A payment class picks its logic with a five-branch if/else instead of separate classes behind one interface. What's the real cost of leaving it that way?
options: Every new payment type means editing that one class and risking the branches that already work.
The code runs slower because if/else is slower than calling an interface method.
Java won't compile a class once it has more than a few if/else branches.
Nothing changes - if/else and separate classes behave identically either way.
why: Right - every new option touches shared code, so one mistake can break a branch that already shipped.
Speed isn't the issue here; both approaches run in about the same time for this kind of logic.
Java has no branch limit - this fails for a design reason, not a compiler one.
They can produce the same output, but only one of them keeps changes contained to new code.
blocks.hint: Think about what you'd have to touch in that one class to add a sixth payment type.
blocks.explain: The interface version adds a class; the if/else version edits a class that already worked and already shipped.

bullets: One interface, many classes - behavior swaps by passing a different object.
The caller never touches new options; it only calls the shared method.
Pick this shape when new behavior keeps showing up and edits keep breaking things.
blocks.remember: New behavior gets a new class, never a new branch.

blocks.say: Time to pick this shape yourself on a rep that actually needs it.

lessons.exitLine: One interface, swapped objects - that's the whole move.
